title: Limits for what actors can do biologically?

commenti.body:
>Could a script include a scene that called for a sharp object to be used to cause the actor to really bleed?

I can assure you that intentional bodily injury is going to go against any contract, union or otherwise. These sorts of things are so easily simulated, whether with props or computers, that there's absolutely no reason professional actors should be intentionally wounding themselves for the camera. There's instances of real injuries making it into a final product, but they're universally accidental injuries that actors continued to act through. DiCaprio's sliced hand in Django Unchained comes to mind.

>I can assure you that intentional bodily injury

It's interesting you phrase it that way and I guess that's part of what my question is getting at. When I go to a medical facility to get my blood drawn, is that an "intentional bodily injury"? 

I say no. I consider bleeding to be a normal bodily function just like urination or sex. But I realize that others might feel differently than me so I am curious to hear about their thoughts.
Your example is medically necessary. No injury in filmmaking is necessary.

Even with something as simple and un-serious as having blood drawn, it would still be an unnecessary medical procedure. I'm sure you could find a blood bank willing to do it, but the union would be woe to let the industry think it's acceptable. Let alone, why should an actor be subjected to something like that when it can be as easily simulated. Yes it's normal to bleed when you get cut, but being cut (or having blood drawn) is not a normal bodily function.

All of this is moot though. If you were to have blood drawn for the camera, there'd be legal requirements that it's done in a medically accredited way, which would undoubtedly cost far more than simply using a $100 prop syringe. This is before we even consider the insurance costs.

As far as excrement goes, I'm sure you could find a couple actors willing to pee so long as their ball and chain aren't explicitly on screen, but why would you want to? Filling them full of water just so you can wait a few hours to hopefully not fuck up your one chance to get a take is a terrible way to run a production. Just give the dude a squeeze bag with a tube and have them face away from the camera.

Furthermore, who wants to see someone actually pee? Or poop, for that matter? Even if these are normal bodily functions, exceedingly few people have any interest in witnessing such actions in a film. There's a reason why this sort of stuff is relegated to wanna-be auteurs and pornhub.

>Furthermore, who wants to see someone actually pee? There's a reason why this sort of stuff is relegated to wanna-be auteurs and pornhub.

It's an interesting question. I'd guess I'd counter by saying that the fact that the fact that porn is popular means that there exists some level of demand for it. Same logic as sex, just not as widespread.

>I'd guess I'd counter by saying that the fact that the fact pron does it means that there exists some level of demand for it. Same logic as sex, just not as widespread. Which is fine, art can be subjective and doesn't have to be for everyone.

I don't disagree that art is subjective and doesn't have to be for everyone, but I will point out that you're asking these questions on a sub focused around commercial Hollywood productions. I'm sure there's more niche subs out there that would take differently to your line of questioning, but I would keep in mind that there's strong reasons why some of the things you ask about aren't done in professional filmmaking. 

Attitudes and practices towards sex on screen are still evolving, which is why I haven't touched on it, but I can assure your that no professional actor wants to be known as the guy that took a shit on screen.
It’s a pivotal scene in the just released The Curse, episode 1. I’m still not sure what I think of the scene.

>Could a script include a scene that called for a sharp object to be used to cause the actor to really bleed? 

\[...\] 

>production could bring a real nurse in to the play the role of a nurse and open up a vein on camera

OP has no business being anywhere close to a professional set. Go away

Kate Winslet notoriously peed on the set of Holy Smoke but the take didn't make it into the final cut. I think with innocuous things like that it really comes down to an actor's comfort level and the director.

The films that make a point of depicting such things are usually known for their auteur directors who seem to do it for attention, re: Von Trier with Nymphomaniac. Which stirs up the old chestnut of being totally naked on film and what it means to both actors and the audience.

There is also a not-so-secret-secret when it comes to drinking scenes, with many actors admitting that they did in fact drink to appear drunk. I heard Pineapple Express was just full of actual smoking, as Seth Rogan is a known pothead.
